quote: [rdi+rsi]: the sum of rdi and rsi
problem: Ch3 taught this reader that square brackets mean memory (Fig 3.2's caption: "Square brackets mean memory", key "[ ] = memory"). Here the brackets are just a sum, and nothing in the drawing, caption or open strip says lea works out the bracketed address without ever reading memory, so the reader cannot fit this with the rule they learned and re-reads.
fix: in the key: "lea computes the address in brackets but never reads memory, so it adds"
reason: Fig 3.2's caption (ch3-isa-p5) does teach 'Square brackets mean memory', and Fig 5.1 then uses brackets for a pure sum. The key does say 'the sum of rdi and rsi', but nothing says why the brackets are not a memory access. Small friction, cheap to remove.
judge_fix: In the Fig 5.1 strip, 'The lea trick' item, append: "The brackets look like Fig 3.2's memory, but `lea` only works out the address and never reads it, so here the address is the sum."

id: fig-5-3 (How it works strip, 'The PDP-7' item; caption ch5-bell-labs-p8)
quote: reaching one character meant shifting and masking
problem: The picture shows two characters packed in one PDP-7 word and raises the question of how B got at one of them. The strip answers with 'shifting' and 'masking', two bit operations the book has not taught (ch2 teaches AND but never calls it a mask, and no earlier section explains a bit shift), so the reader cannot explain how it was done.
fix: plain words, e.g. 'pulling one character out of its word took extra instructions'
reason: 'Shifting and masking' appears nowhere earlier in the book. ch2 teaches AND but never calls it a mask, and no section explains a bit shift. The phrase is the strip's whole answer to how B reached one of two packed characters, so the reader gets jargon where the answer should be.
judge_fix: In the Fig 5.3 strip, 'The PDP-7' item, replace 'reaching one character meant shifting and masking' with: "reaching one character meant extra instructions to pull it out of its word."

quote: Every byte of dynamic memory your C program uses, you allocated.
problem: 'Dynamic memory' is never tied to the heap. p2 only says 'heap memory requires explicit requests', so the reader cannot tell which memory the opening rule covers (the stack also changes as the program runs) until they work it out at p2.
fix: say 'heap memory' instead of 'dynamic memory', or add '(the heap)'
reason: 'Dynamic memory' appears nowhere else in the book and is not tied to the heap until p2. The stack also changes while the program runs, so on a plain reading the opening rule ('you allocated every byte') is false for stack memory. 'Heap' was taught in ch3-stack-p2 and p4.
judge_fix: p1: "Every byte of heap memory your C program uses, you allocated." (leave the rest unchanged)

quote: so the allocator must ask the kernel for more
problem: Fig 5.6 shows 400 bytes free and a 300-byte request, so this reader asks why the allocator cannot slide p3 and p5 aside to join the free pieces. Nothing says a chunk in use can never move because the program holds its address, so 'must' does not follow, and the strip's 'fenced by a chunk still in use' leaves the same question open.
fix: one clause: a chunk in use cannot be moved, because the program holds its address
reason: Fragmentation only follows if chunks in use cannot be moved. The picture shows 400 free bytes and a failed 300-byte request, so a newcomer will ask why p3 and p5 cannot slide aside. Nowhere is the reason given: the program holds each chunk's address. The strip says 'fenced by a chunk still in use' but not why a fence is permanent.
judge_fix: p3: "...the heap becomes a patchwork of chunks, each marked in use or free (a chunk in use never moves, because the program holds its address), with the free ones linked into the allocator's free list, which it searches for room."

quote: Touching that page raises a hardware fault.
problem: The NULL subsection (p5, Fig 5.9, and its strip's 'a NULL access always traps') shows a guaranteed crash, so this reader cannot say why NULL dereference is on the undefined list when p1 said the standard requires 'not even a crash', or what the optimiser does with it; the null-check deduction that the Fig 5.8 strip (-fno-delete-null-pointer-checks) and p7 ('switch specific deductions off') turn off is never shown.
fix: one sentence joining it to the argument: the trap is the OS's doing, not a promise of C; an optimiser that sees a pointer dereferenced may assume it is not NULL and delete a later NULL check
reason: p1 says undefined behaviour means 'not even a crash'. NULL dereference is on the list, yet this subsection and its strip ('a NULL access always traps') present a guaranteed crash and never say why it counts as undefined. The reader cannot reconcile the two. The strip and p7 also refer to the kernel's -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks switch, whose effect has not been shown.
judge_fix: Append to p5: "That crash is the operating system's doing, not a promise of C. The standard leaves the dereference undefined, so an optimiser that sees `*p` may assume `p` is not NULL and delete a later `if (p == NULL)` check, as Fig 5.8 deleted the overflow test."

quote: objects on top of C's speed
problem: "Objects" in the programming sense is never defined, here or earlier, but it is the whole of what the first wave added (the picture's label "keep the speed, add objects"). The only nearby mention, ch5-pointers-p7's vtables of Chapter 6, does not explain it, so this reader cannot say what Objective-C and C++ added.
fix: half a sentence: an object bundles data with the functions that work on it (Chapter 6)
reason: 'Objects' is the entire content of the first wave and the label 'keep the speed, add objects' is never glossed. Chapter 6 explains it, but this chapter's only mention of the term is the figure label and caption. A half-line in the closed strip fixes it at no cost to the picture.
judge_fix: Fig 5.11 strip, 'First wave' item, prepend: "An object bundles data with the functions that work on it (Chapter 6)." then keep the existing sentence.

quote: Go and Swift manage memory for you
problem: The second wave is defined by a runtime that manages memory, yet the third wave's Go and Swift also manage memory for you (and ch3-overflow-p9 said Go has a runtime). So this reader cannot tell what puts them under "keep the speed" and not the second wave. The old caption's step (the second wave ran on a virtual machine, trading raw performance for safety) is no longer there.
fix: say the second wave's runtime stands between program and processor and costs speed, while Go and Swift compile straight to machine code
reason: The wave labels do separate 'keep the syntax' from 'keep the speed'. But the third-wave strip says only that Go and Swift 'manage memory for you', which is the second wave's defining trait, and ch3-overflow-p9 says Go has a runtime. Nothing says what keeps them in the speed wave. p2 supplies the answer, compiling straight to machine code, and the strip does not use it.
judge_fix: Fig 5.11 strip, 'Third wave' item: "Rust proves memory safety at compile time through ownership; Go and Swift compile to machine code, as C does, but manage memory for you; Zig keeps manual control with fewer traps."

quote: Stroustrup, who said that, was reflecting on his own creation.
problem: Nothing in the book so far says Stroustrup created C++. The old Fig 5.11 caption said "Stroustrup's C++"; the redrawn figure, its strip and the prose dropped it. So "his own creation" points at something unnamed, and both the quote's irony and the hand-off to Chapter 6 depend on a link the reader has to guess.
fix: name it: "his own creation, C++"
reason: Nothing in ch5 says Stroustrup made C++. The figure lists C++ (1985) without his name and the quote is attributed to him separately. 'His own creation' therefore points at something the reader must guess, and the hand-off to Chapter 6 rests on that link.
judge_fix: p6: "Stroustrup, who said that, was reflecting on his own creation, C++."

quote: The TLS library that secured your connection is C.
problem: For most readers in 2026 this is false. Chrome, Edge and Android use BoringSSL. Its libssl has been C++ since 2017, and the commit "crypto: switch to C++" (boringssl.googlesource.com 5813c2c, 30 Oct 2024) "switches nearly all of BoringSSL to use C++"; only the public interface stays C. Apple's Network.framework also builds its TLS on an internal BoringSSL. Only Firefox's NSS is still C. The sentence sits in a list of plain facts, so the reader takes it as one.
fix: "OpenSSL, the TLS library behind most web servers, is C." (Or: "The TLS library that secured your connection is C, or C++ behind a C interface.")
reason: Checked: BoringSSL commit 5813c2c 'crypto: switch to C++' moves nearly all of BoringSSL to C++ (C ABI kept), and ssl/ was converted piecemeal from 2017. Chrome, Edge and Android clients, and Cloudflare/Google servers, therefore use a C++ TLS library. OpenSSL (Fig 5.10's example) and NSS are C. The sentence sits in a list of flat facts, right after 'the browser is C++', so a plain claim about 'the' library is wrong for most readers.
judge_fix: Replace the sentence with: "The TLS library behind most web servers, OpenSSL, is C." Source: boringssl.googlesource.com/boringssl/+/5813c2c10c73d800f1b0d890a7d74ff973abbffc

quote: In a windowless room at Bell Labs in 1969, Ken Thompson found a discarded PDP-7
problem: No source I could find mentions a windowless room; it reads as invented colour. Ritchie's own account ("The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System", 1979) says Thompson found "a little-used PDP-7 computer with an excellent display processor": it belonged to another department and had not been thrown out. The section also calls the machine three different things: "discarded" (p1), "unused" (p3) and "discarded" in the title.
fix: "At Bell Labs in 1969, Ken Thompson found a little-used PDP-7 and started writing a programming environment for himself." (Source: pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.828/2005/readings/ritchie79evolution.html)
reason: Ritchie 1979 ('The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System'), checked: 'Thompson [found] a little-used PDP-7 computer with an excellent display processor'. Nothing about a windowless room (unsourced colour) and nothing about it being discarded. The book also calls the same machine 'discarded' (title, p1) and 'salvaged ... unused' (p3). Those imply a cast-off; Ritchie's machine belonged to another group. Folds in #10.
judge_fix: p1: "At Bell Labs in 1969, Ken Thompson found a little-used PDP-7 and started writing a programming environment for himself." Title: "Two men, a spare minicomputer, four years." p3: replace "Thompson salvaged an unused PDP-7" with "Thompson took over a little-used PDP-7". Source: pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.828/2005/readings/ritchie79evolution.html

quote: In 1972 Ritchie added types, so the compiler knew a `char` (one byte) from an `int`
problem: Ritchie dates the types to 1971. In "The Development of the C Language" (1993) he writes: "In 1971 I began to extend the B language by adding a character type". That interim language was called NB. He renamed it C only after "creating the type system", and the most creative period was 1972. The types came first and the name followed. Fig 5.2's "1972: C" is fine as a date for C itself.
fix: "In 1971 and 1972 Ritchie added types, so the compiler knew a `char` (one byte) from an `int` (a word), and called the result *C*: the language that comes after B." (Source: plan9.io/cm/cs/who/dmr/chist.html)
reason: Ritchie's 'The Development of the C Language', checked: 'In 1971 I began to extend the B language by adding a character type' (NB, which already had int, char, arrays, pointers). He renamed it C only after building the fuller type system; the most creative period was 1972. So 'In 1972 Ritchie added types' misdates the first types. 'By 1972' is true and keeps Fig 5.2's 1972: C.
judge_fix: "By 1972 Ritchie had added types, so the compiler knew a `char` (one byte) from an `int` (a word), and he called the result *C*: the language that comes after B." Source: plan9.io/cm/cs/who/dmr/chist.html

quote: x86: 1 to 15 bytes each · ARM, RISC-V: always 4
problem: RISC-V instructions are not always 4 bytes. Its standard compressed extension (part of RV64GC, the default target of Linux distributions) has 2-byte forms, and the figure's own strip says both instructions "shrink to 2 bytes each". The drawn label and the caption ("the fixed 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V") contradict that strip. ARM64 is always 4 bytes.
fix: Label: "x86: 1 to 15 bytes · ARM64: always 4 · RISC-V: 4 (2 compressed)". Caption: "…x86's variable-length bytes against the 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V."
reason: Real contradiction inside the figure: the drawn label says RISC-V is 'always 4', while its own strip says the compressed extension shrinks both instructions to 2 bytes. RISC-V with the C extension (the default in RV64GC Linux) has 2-byte forms. ARM64 is always 4. Fig 5.1 is not in kept_original.
judge_fix: Label: "x86: 1 to 15 bytes each · ARM64: always 4 · RISC-V: 4, or 2 compressed" (check it still fits at 375 px; if not, "x86: 1 to 15 bytes · ARM64: 4 · RISC-V: 4 or 2"). Caption: "x86's variable-length bytes against the 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V" (drop 'fixed'). Also the <desc> phrase 'fixed 4 bytes of ARM and RISC-V' becomes 'the 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V'.

quote: Operating systems leave the lowest pages unmapped on purpose (Linux's `mmap_min_addr`), so a NULL access always traps.
problem: "Always" overstates it, and the chapter itself shows why. A NULL dereference is undefined behaviour (ch5-ub-p2), so the compiler may delete the access or the check before it. That is why Linux builds with -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks (Fig 5.8's strip), after the 2009 tun-driver exploit. Also, root can lower mmap_min_addr, and NULL plus a large offset (p->field, a[i]) lands beyond the unmapped guard.
fix: "…(Linux's `mmap_min_addr`), so an access at or near address 0 traps instead of reading data."
reason: 'Always traps' contradicts the chapter's own account: p1 says UB can be 'not even a crash', and Fig 5.8's strip names -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks because the optimiser can delete null accesses. Also root can lower mmap_min_addr, and NULL plus a large offset lands past the unmapped page. What holds is the hardware fact about address 0 and the lowest pages. Cheap fix. Folds in #15.
judge_fix: Fig 5.9 strip: "Operating systems leave the lowest pages unmapped on purpose (Linux's `mmap_min_addr`), so an access at or near address 0 traps instead of reading data."

problem: p6 "Its types are the byte and the processor's own word" and p7 "an `int` (a word)" are true of the PDP-11, where `int` was its 16-bit word. They are not true of today's 64-bit targets, including all three in Fig 5.1: there `int` is 32 bits while the registers are 64. The section's own figure shows this: its strip says 64-bit RISC-V's `addw` "adds 32-bit `int`s", the ARM line uses the 32-bit `w` registers, and ch3-call-p3 says the 32-bit `int` arrives in EDI/ESI, the lower halves of the 64-bit registers. Suggest scoping to the PDP-11 ("on the PDP-11, an `int` was one word") or to a type of word size rather than `int`.
reason: p6 states as a general design fact that C's types are 'the byte and the processor's own word'. On the three 64-bit targets of Fig 5.1 and in Fig 5.4 an `int` is 4 bytes while the registers are 8, so the book's own figures show 'int is the word' is false today. p7's '`int` (a word)' sits in a 1972 PDP-11 context and is fine; only p6 is a general claim. K&R's own phrase is 'the natural size of integers on the host machine'.
judge_fix: p6: "Its types are the byte and an integer of the machine's natural size, its `if` statements and loops become conditional jumps, ..." Leave p7 unchanged.

problem: ch5-bell-labs-p3, 'He started writing a small operating system for it, partly to play a space-travel game he had ported from Multics' (low): Ritchie's account gives a different order. Space Travel went from Multics to a GECOS Fortran version, and then Thompson and Ritchie rewrote it to run on the bare PDP-7, cross-assembled on GECOS, before any operating system existed. Only after that did Thompson start the file system and the OS, to get a better place to work. The game did not need the OS. The 'written to play the game' version is the popular retelling.
reason: Ritchie 1979, checked: Space Travel was written on Multics, then Fortran for GECOS, then Thompson and Ritchie rewrote it for the bare PDP-7 (cross-assembled on GECOS, paper tapes), and only 'soon' after did Thompson begin the file system and the OS. The game did not need the OS; the OS grew out of the PDP-7 work. The book's 'to play a space-travel game' is the popular retelling. Cheap to repair.
judge_fix: p3: replace "He started writing a small operating system for it, partly to play a space-travel game he had ported from Multics, partly to have an environment to work in." with "He and Ritchie first rewrote a space-travel game of his, written on Multics, to run on it. Then Thompson began a small operating system there, to have a better environment to work in." Source: pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.828/2005/readings/ritchie79evolution.html

problem: ch5-pointers-p4 (Fig 5.4 caption): the first sentence shows the char pointer moving 1 byte, then the second says `p + 1` 'always means the next element, never the next byte'. For a `char *` the next element is the next byte. The claim holds only if `p` means the figure's `int *p`, so 'never' reads as an overstatement. A careful reader may stop briefly at this wording; it does not break the argument.
reason: The caption's first sentence says the `char` pointer moves 1 byte, then concludes `p + 1` means 'never the next byte'. For a `char *` the next element is the next byte, so the caption contradicts the first row of its own figure. p3 is fine because it is conditioned on `int *p`. A newcomer checking picture against caption will stop here.
judge_fix: Caption, last clause: "The compiler scales pointer arithmetic by the size of the type, so `p + 1` always means the next element, whatever its size."

problem: Fig 5.11 How it works, third wave: "Rust proves memory safety at compile time through ownership" overstates it. Ownership and borrow checking rule out use-after-free and aliasing errors at compile time, but array bounds are checked while the program runs (an out-of-bounds index panics). ch3-overflow-p9 already told the reader exactly that ("a Rust panic"), so the strip contradicts the book's own earlier account.
reason: 'Proves memory safety at compile time through ownership' overstates it: ownership and borrowing rule out use-after-free and aliasing at compile time, but array bounds are checked at run time (ch3-overflow-p9 shows the Rust panic). The book's own Fig 5.7 strip words it correctly ('reject use-after-free at compile time'), so Fig 5.11 contradicts the book's own precision.
judge_fix: Fig 5.11 third-wave strip: "*Third wave.* Rust rules out use-after-free and data races at compile time through ownership, and checks array bounds as the program runs; Go and Swift manage memory for you; Zig keeps manual control with fewer traps."

quote: Its bytes are what forced types into the language.
problem: The Fig 5.3 strip repeats what its own caption says ("which is why C, unlike B, gave its pointers types"). It also repeats ch5-portability-p7: "B, its language, had a single type, the word" restates p7's "B, which saw only words".
fix: In the strip, cut "Its bytes are what forced types into the language." from "The PDP-11" bullet. In "The PDP-7" bullet keep only "Bell Labs' machine had 8K words of 18 bits; reaching one character meant shifting and masking."
reason: The sentence 'Its bytes are what forced types into the language.' in the Fig 5.3 'The PDP-11' bullet restates the figure's own caption, which ends 'which is why C, unlike B, gave its pointers types'. The PDP-7 bullet's shifting-and-masking point is new and should stay.
judge_fix: Cut only that sentence. The bullet becomes: "*The PDP-11.* A 16-bit design with byte addresses, eight registers and regular addressing modes." Leave the PDP-7 bullet as written.

quote: so `p + 1` always means the next element, never the next byte
problem: The caption says "never the next byte" one clause after saying that the char pointer moves 1 byte. For a char, the next element is the next byte, so the absolute claim contradicts the figure. The sentence also repeats ch5-pointers-p3 ("The compiler scales the arithmetic for you").
fix: Cut the caption's second sentence so it reads: "Three pointers start at 0x100 and take the same step, `++`: the `char` pointer moves 1 byte, the `int` pointer 4, the `double` pointer 8."
reason: For a `char` pointer the next element is the next byte, so 'never the next byte' contradicts the caption's own first sentence. The clause also repeats p3 ('The compiler scales the arithmetic for you').
judge_fix: Cut the caption's second sentence: "Three pointers start at 0x100 and take the same step, `++`: the `char` pointer moves 1 byte, the `int` pointer 4, the `double` pointer 8."

quote: The C standard defines `a[i]` as `*(a + i)`: add `i` elements to the address, then read what is there.
problem: ch5-pointers-p5, directly above, opens with the same sentence ("The C standard defines `a[i]` ... to mean exactly `*(a + i)`: indexing is shorthand for pointer arithmetic"). The caption also ends on the same conclusion, and the strip's "The rule" bullet states the definition a third time. Under the brief's "say it once" rule, the prose keeps it and the caption names the picture.
fix: Caption: "`a[2]` rewritten step by step down to the 99 stored at 0x108. `2[a]`, legal but never written, reads the same 99, because addition commutes."
reason: The Fig 5.5 caption's first sentence repeats p5 almost word for word. The brief's rule is that the prose keeps it and the caption names the picture. The 'The rule' strip bullet quotes C99 §6.5.2.1 and is a source citation, so it stays.
judge_fix: Caption: "`a[2]` rewritten step by step down to the 99 stored at 0x108. `2[a]`, legal but never written, reads the same 99, because addition commutes."

quote: With the compressed extension both instructions shrink to 2 bytes each.
problem: The drawn key says "ARM, RISC-V: always 4" and the caption says "the fixed 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V". The strip then says the RISC-V instructions can be 2 bytes. A careful reader stops on "always".
fix: Delete this sentence from the strip's "The `w` in `addw`" bullet so it reads: "On 64-bit RISC-V it adds 32-bit `int`s."
reason: The drawn key says 'ARM, RISC-V: always 4' and the caption says 'fixed 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V'. The strip then says RISC-V's compressed extension makes both instructions 2 bytes. That is true: addw becomes c.addw and ret becomes c.jr ra. So 'always 4' is wrong for RISC-V, and deleting the strip sentence would hide the contradiction without fixing the figure. The two encodings drawn are the base 4-byte forms.
judge_fix: Make the figure true. Drawn key: "x86: 1 to 15 bytes each · ARM: always 4 · RISC-V: 4, or 2 compressed". If that does not fit the SVG width, use "ARM, RISC-V: 4 bytes here". Caption: change "the fixed 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V" to "the 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V". Keep the strip sentence about the compressed extension.

quote: A leak loses the last pointer to memory that is still allocated, so the heap only grows
problem: The caption repeats ch5-malloc-p5 almost word for word: the leak until the OS kills the process, and the use-after-free whose chunk goes to the next caller and gets overwritten. p1 had already given the same two outcomes, so the reader gets the consequences three times in one section.
fix: Caption names the picture: "Above, three chunks lose their only pointer and the heap only grows. Below, `p` outlives `free(p)`, the same chunk goes to `q`, and a write through `p` lands in `q`'s data."
reason: The Fig 5.7 caption nearly repeats ch5-malloc-p5: the leak until the OS ends the process, and the chunk handed to the next caller and overwritten. The brief says the caption names the picture.
judge_fix: Caption: "In the leak, three chunks lose their only pointer and the heap only grows. In the use-after-free, `p` outlives `free(p)`, the same chunk goes to `q`, and a write through `p` lands in `q`'s data."

quote: C makes you the bookkeeper. There is no garbage collector.
problem: Two clipped dramatic fragments close the lead. The second relies on "garbage collector", which is first explained in p7 of this section and appears nowhere earlier in the book. At this point a baseline reader cannot tell what is missing.
fix: Replace both sentences with: "C makes you the bookkeeper: nothing in the language frees memory for you." p7 then introduces garbage collection where it is explained.
reason: 'There is no garbage collector' is the first use of the term in the book. Part I has no mention, and the first Part II occurrence is this paragraph. It is not explained until p7. A baseline reader cannot tell what is missing, so it is a term-order defect and the sentence is a clipped fragment.
judge_fix: Replace the last two sentences with: "C makes you the bookkeeper: nothing in the language frees memory for you." p7 then introduces garbage collection where it is explained.

quote: converts it into a signal called `SIGSEGV` ("segmentation violation"), which by default kills the process
problem: Chapter 4 has already taught this whole path. ch4-vm-p11 says "using an unmapped address such as 0 (NULL) ... The kernel sends the offending process a SIGSEGV signal ... the famous 'segmentation fault' message", Fig 4.9 draws it, and ch4-ipc teaches signals. p5 presents SIGSEGV as new, and Fig 5.9's caption and its "Why address 0 faults" bullet repeat p5 again. The strip even admits "This is the 'invalid' exit of the page-fault tree in Fig 4.9".
fix: Make p5 a recall: "A pointer with the value `0` (or `NULL`, C's name for it) points nowhere: the kernel leaves the first page of every process unmapped, so touching it takes the 'invalid' exit of Fig 4.9 and ends in `SIGSEGV`, the `Segmentation fault (core dumped)` that has greeted C programmers for fifty years." Fig 5.9 caption: "One write through NULL, followed from user code through the MMU, the kernel and the signal to the shell's message."
reason: ch4-vm-p12 already teaches unmapped address 0 (NULL), then SIGSEGV, then the 'segmentation fault' message. Fig 4.9 draws the path, and the Fig 5.9 strip admits 'This is the invalid exit of the page-fault tree in Fig 4.9'. p5 presents all of it as new, and the Fig 5.9 caption repeats p5.
judge_fix: p5: "A pointer with the value `0` (or `NULL`, C's name for it) points nowhere: the kernel leaves the first page of every process unmapped, so touching it takes the 'invalid' exit of Fig 4.9 and ends in `SIGSEGV`, the `Segmentation fault (core dumped)` that has greeted C programmers for fifty years." Fig 5.9 caption: "One write through NULL, followed from user code through the MMU, the kernel and the signal to the shell's message." Keep the strip bullets.

quote: Operating systems leave the lowest pages unmapped on purpose (Linux's `mmap_min_addr`), so a NULL access always traps.
problem: The section has just taught that dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behaviour, with "no requirement at all on what happens, not even a crash" (p1, p2). Fig 5.8's strip names -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks, which exists because optimisers act on that assumption. "Always traps" contradicts both, and the NULL subsection never ties back to the UB argument it sits inside.
fix: "...so a NULL access that the compiled code actually performs traps. Because the access is undefined, the optimiser may first remove it, or a NULL check near it."
reason: The section has just taught that a null dereference is undefined behaviour and that the optimiser may delete code on that basis. The Fig 5.8 strip even names -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks. 'A NULL access always traps' overstates it: the compiler may remove the access, and mmap_min_addr is configurable. The hardware fact is fine, but the word 'always' is not.
judge_fix: "Operating systems leave the lowest pages unmapped on purpose (Linux's `mmap_min_addr`), so a NULL access that actually reaches the hardware traps. Being undefined behaviour, it may be removed by the compiler before it gets there."

quote: not "the program might crash" but "the program's behaviour is no longer governed by the source you wrote."
problem: The strip combines a "not X but Y" reveal with an aphorism closer ("This is the cost of C's performance."), and it restates p1 ("places no requirement at all on what happens, not even a crash").
fix: "*Undefined behaviour:* once a program breaks one of these promises, its behaviour is no longer governed by the source you wrote, and the optimiser is entitled to act on that." Drop the last sentence.
reason: The strip has a 'not X but Y' reveal and an aphorism closer ('This is the cost of C's performance.'). The Pass 29-30 brief names both as AI-style defects. The first clause also echoes p1 ('not even a crash'). Restating the take-away is an insight strip's job and is not the defect.
judge_fix: Keep the bold lead. Body: "Once a program breaks one of these promises, its behaviour is no longer governed by the source you wrote, and the optimiser is entitled to act on that." Drop the last sentence.

quote: Linux is C. macOS XNU and Windows NT are mostly C. The Python interpreter is C.
problem: The paragraph is a run of clipped fragments with an aphorism closer ("C is so deep in the foundations that it has become invisible."). Its inventory (Python interpreter, TLS library, Linux) is what Fig 5.10 draws and captions just below, and the chapter lead already says the same about the kernel, browser and runtime. "TLS" is also not taught until Chapter 11.
fix: "Every five years, someone writes a clickbait piece announcing that C is dying, and every five years more C runs in production than before. Linux is written in C, macOS's XNU kernel and Windows NT mostly so, and the browser rendering this page in C++, C's best-known descendant. Fig 5.10 follows one Python program down through the C beneath it."
